subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: perfectionism stalls the first version [Pitfall]
passage: For four weeks Gopika had been building a timetable planner in Python, and she had nothing that ran. Every time she looked at her code she saw mess: a function called do_stuff, files named badly. So she deleted it and started again. She renamed folders planner_final, planner_final2, planner_new. She read three style guides and picked a colour theme for her editor. The school coding fair was in nine days. Farhan, beside her, said, “Just get one button working.” “It'll look bad.” On the morning of the fair Gopika had a folder of tidy, empty files, and on the next table sat Farhan's rough, slightly ugly calculator, working.

qa.q: How many weeks had Gopika been building the planner?
What might Gopika be feeling when she says it will look bad?
qa.a: Embarrassed and afraid of judgment: fear of messy code keeps her from finishing anything.

qa.q: What could Gopika do instead, and why?
qa.a: Build a rough working version first and tidy it afterwards, since something that runs can be improved while empty files cannot.

qa.q: How does Gopika's habit look to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan sees someone capable stuck restarting when a rough version could already run, so Farhan urges Gopika to get one button working.

grounding: A teen keeps restarting because the structure feels messy, spends a month on setup and never reaches a working first version.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: perfectionism stalls the first version [Pitfall]
passage:
For the fourth time in a month, Gurleen dragged the whole project folder to the bin. Her homework-planner program had nine empty files, a colour scheme and a page of rules for naming variables, but not a single screen that did anything.
“It's messy,” she told her mother, who had come to call her for dinner in their Andheri flat. “If the base is wrong, everything after it will be wrong.”
At school the next day, Thomas showed the computer class his own planner. It was ugly: grey buttons, one screen, a spelling mistake in the title. But you could add homework and tick it off, and three people asked him to send it to them.
Gurleen watched, jaw tight. The teacher had fixed demo day for that Friday. She had a folder of perfect names and nothing to show.

qa.q: What did Gurleen's project have after a month?
qa.a: Nine empty files, a colour scheme and a page of rules for naming variables, but no screen that did anything.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's tight jaw during the demo suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated and perhaps envious, watching a rough but working planner win attention while her careful setup had nothing to show.

qa.q: What would you change first in Gurleen's approach?
qa.a: Build one ugly screen that adds and ticks off homework before touching names or colours, then tidy the structure once something works.

qa.q: How might Thomas see the difference between the two planners?
qa.a: Thomas probably sees the grey, misspelled version as a start that can be improved, because people are already using it.

grounding: Shows a teen restarting her program again and again over messy structure and naming, and reaching demo day with no working version.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: perfectionism stalls the first version [Pitfall]
passage:
“Bhavna, fest registrations closed yesterday. Did your site go live?”
“No, Ishita Di. I rebuilt the folders again. The names were inconsistent.”
“Again? What's that, the fifth rebuild?”
“Sixth. If I launch something messy, people will judge it.”
“Who's judging? Show me what it does right now.”
Bhavna turned the laptop round. A title. A blank page underneath.
“This is a month of work?”
“The setup took time! Folder structure, naming, a style guide...”
“And the fest committee?”
Bhavna looked away. “They used a paper form in the end. The office said sorting it took two free periods.”
“So the tidy version cost them two periods and cost you the chance.”
“I know.” Her voice went small. “I just wanted it right the first time.”
“Nobody's first version is right, Bhavu. That's why it's called the first.”

qa.q: How did the fest committee take registrations in the end?
What was Bhavna feeling when her voice went small?
qa.a: Bhavna felt ashamed and disappointed, seeing that wanting it right the first time had stopped anything from getting done 😔

qa.q: What else could Bhavna have tried a month ago?
qa.a: She could have put up a plain one-page form in the first week and cleaned up the structure later, once the committee was already using it.

qa.q: How does the month look to Ishita?
qa.a: To Ishita it looks like effort spent in the wrong place; she cares, but is blunt because the committee paid for the delay.

grounding: Shows perfectionism about folders and naming stalling a first version for a month, with a real cost when a paper form replaces the site.
